Lessons.Title: Using Function Notation to Describe Rules (Part 2)
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning objective: evaluate and solve equations involving linear functions, distinguish constant-rate graphs from nonlinear graphs and use graphing technology when actually accessible. Original Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 4 Lesson 5, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/4/5/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). The source introduces 'linear function' and includes an optional technology activity; it is not simply a second copy of Lesson 4.

Independent first-party temperature-like model, without asserting physical calibration: T(t)=18+1.5t degrees for elapsed minutes t∈[0,10]. It is linear because each minute increases predicted output by1.5 degrees. At t=4, T=24; solve T(t)=27 to find t=6. A straight graph passes through (0,18),(4,24),(6,27).

Contrast a nonlinear function Q(t)=t²+2 on t≥0: Q(0)=2, Q(1)=3, Q(2)=6, Q(3)=11. First differences are1,3,5 rather than constant; its graph curves. For a constant-rate function, average rates between any two distinct inputs in the domain equal the slope. When solving equations using a graph, intersections with horizontal output line correspond to inputs with that output.

Student task: generate both graphs and compare their rates, solve two target-output equations by algebra and graph reading, and document whether real graphing technology was used or drawings were manual. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for accurate evaluation, inverse input-solving, mathematical evidence of linearity/nonlinearity and correct labelled graphs plus technology disclosure.

KeyConcepts.Title: Linear function
KeyConcepts.Definition: A function whose output changes by a constant amount per equal input increment.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Its graph is a straight line with constant slope.

KeyConcepts.Title: Nonlinear function
KeyConcepts.Definition: A rule whose input-output change does not have one fixed rate across its domain.

KeyConcepts.Title: Solving a target output
KeyConcepts.Definition: The equation f(t)=k asks which inputs yield output k.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use algebra or where graph crosses y=k.

WorkedExamples.Title: Evaluate and solve a linear function
WorkedExamples.Question: Given T(t)=18+1.5t, find T(4) and when T=27.
WorkedExamples.Method: Represent the function with its stated input/output domain and verify the mathematical assertion.

WorkedExamples.Title: Verify a constant rate
WorkedExamples.Question: Find average rate of T between t=0 and4, and4 and6.
WorkedExamples.Method: Represent the function with its stated input/output domain and verify the mathematical assertion.
Steps: The rates match: the model is linear.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Rate constant at1.5 output units per minute.

WorkedExamples.Title: Identify a nonlinear rule
WorkedExamples.Question: Given Q(t)=t²+2, evaluate at t=0,1,2,3 and compare equal-step differences.
WorkedExamples.Method: Represent the function with its stated input/output domain and verify the mathematical assertion.
Steps: Because differences differ for unit steps, rate is not constant.
The graph is curved rather than a straight line.
WorkedExamples.Check: Nonconstant differences disprove linearity on tested domain.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Function notation applies to nonlinear and piecewise rules too.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check rate of change before labeling linear.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming an authored graph proves actual software use
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A text table is not evidence of a tool session.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Disclose manual versus authentic technology work.

SummaryPoints: A linear function changes at constant rate and has a straight-line graph.
Use f(t)=k to determine inputs for a desired output.
Nonlinear functions have varying rates across intervals.
Teacher evaluates graph and explanation, with truthful technology evidence.
